strengths: Addresses an important question: why distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL. The discussion connects relevant work on CDRL, fitted Q-iteration, and maximum-entropy RL.
The conditional return-density decomposition and categorical/histogram loss correspondence provide a potentially useful perspective on distributional critic objectives.

Experiments cover eight Atari games and several continuous-control tasks, with multiple seeds and ablations of distributional losses and policy entropy. The authors acknowledge the restricted theoretical scope and inconsistent performance advantages.
weaknesses: The central explanatory link is unsupported. Equations (7)–(9) introduce a cross-entropy reward bonus, but decomposing a critic loss does not establish that existing C51 or DSAC optimizes this augmented return. The standard distributional Bellman operator preserves expectations; the manuscript needs a derivation connecting its new objective to the behavior being explained.

The DERAC derivation contains a substantive algebraic error. In Appendix I, writing δ for the expected-value Bellman residual, expanding (δ + sqrt(τH))² produces the cross term 2sqrt(τ)E[δsqrt(H)]. Equation (36) instead writes E[δH] and then removes it. Bellman-residual orthogonality does not generally hold for arbitrary learned critics and separate target networks. Consequently, Equation (10) is not established as equivalent to the proposed augmented Bellman objective.

The convergence argument in Appendix H treats the augmented reward as fixed while changing policies. However, its target distribution depends on the policy, and its cross-entropy depends on the learned critic. Boundedness alone does not justify contraction or monotone policy improvement under these changes. The proof supports a frozen-bonus setting, rather than the full claimed procedure.

Proposition 4.3 concerns idealized limiting minimizers under strong representation assumptions; it does not establish equivalent cross-entropy and squared-error learning dynamics for finite-bin neural critics. This distinction matters for explaining practical C51–DQN differences. Additionally, Equation (32) incorrectly calls its error o(Δ): the displayed expression lies between Δ/4 and Δ/2, so it is Θ(Δ).

Cross-entropy is not solely a measure of distribution mismatch: H(μ,q) = H(μ) + KL(μ||q). It can remain large when q perfectly matches μ. Consequently, the proposed bonus can reward irreducible return randomness, and the claims about targeting poorly learned distributions require a clearer distinction between environmental randomness and uncertainty from insufficient knowledge.

The experiments demonstrate performance differences without isolating the claimed exploration mechanism. Section 6.1 replaces the full target distribution with the residual distribution μ, changing the learning target rather than cleanly removing a regularizer. There are no direct measurements of exploration coverage or uncertainty reduction, or controls separating these effects from representation and optimization changes. Learning-curve interpolation also cannot substantiate the tabular convergence theorem.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the supplied pseudocode and shared hyperparameters. Categorical support bounds, Atari preprocessing and exploration settings, the precise mapping between the two epsilon parameters, and the meaning of shaded uncertainty bands are insufficiently specified. These gaps hinder verification of the central ablations.
